newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-ARCO mulling coal sale options.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ARCO mulling coal sale options.

text.p: ARCO is still considering whether to float shares or undertake a trade sale for its coal assets, but expects to come to a decision within a few months, chief executive Mike Bowlin said in an interview.
"We are now in the final throes of looking at what a spun-off company would look like in the market," Bowlin said.
ARCO earlier this year said that it would sell its coal assets, mainly in the U.S. and Australia, which analysts have valued at up to $9.30 per ARCO share, or a total of $1.5 billion.
Bowlin said it also was possible that the sale of the Australian and U.S. assets would proceed in different ways, one as a trade sale, one as a float.
"We expect to complete the deals by the end of this year," Bowlin said.

Asked whether ARCO felt threatened by the proposed West Coast downstream alliance between Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co, the refining arm of Royal Dutch/Shell, Bowlin said that the announcement of their alliance had been a "wake up call for the industry".

"We have evaluated and been in discussions on a number of joint ventures and while I am not pleased with current margins on the West Coast, if I take a five year period of time then I see a business which has performed well for ARCO," he said.
Bowlin said that the purchase of 260 Thrifty gas stations in California earlier this year showed that ARCO wanted to retain its pre-eminent retailing position on the West Coast.
He said that he expects the company's increased focus on exploration and production, especially growing overseas reserves, to be rewarded by Wall Street.
Earlier this year, ARCO took a number of actions, the planned coal sale, a stock split and performance-related shares for executives which Wall Street applauded.
The company also said it plans four percent growth in energy production to the year 2001 and a doubling of international reserves, with key areas in China, Indonesia, Russia, Algeria and Venezuela.
Bowlin said that one of the keys to ARCO's overseas growth was its pairing with Russia's LUKoil. ARCO holds an eight percent stake in LUKoil and a 46 percent interest in joint partnership, LUKArco.

"We do not intend to get involved with LUKoil's plans outside the Former Soviet Union, it is their access to reserves there, in the Caspian that attracted us. We have the technical, capital and operating knowhow, they have the land position and the political connections," Bowlin said.
LUKArco has a stake in the giant Tengiz oilfield, which aims to be producing 180,000 barrels per day by the end of this year, as well as a holding in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium.
Bowlin said that ARCO has no intention of increasing its eight percent stake in LUKoil itself when the Russian company undertakes another overseas share sale later this year.

Also overseas, ARCO aims to prove up its Weriagar and Berau fields in Indonesia. Bowlin said that the company expects to build at least two liquified natural gas pipelines, producing some six million tonnes of LNG per year.
Domestically, ARCO says that its ability to turn around production declines from the Alaskan North Slope had been key to altering investor perceptions of the company.

"I felt for some time that many people looked at ARCO and saw a glass that was half empty and we really think we have one that is half full. There has been a turnaround in our prospects in the past couple of years and we are now seeing rewards," Bowlin said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
